case.name: Harbour Lane Capital (fictional)
case.summary: A UK merchant cash advance (MCA) provider. Merchants receive a lump sum and repay a fixed total (advance x factor rate) through a holdback: a fixed % of their daily card takings. Most deals come through brokers; about a third of volume is renewals.
assumptions: List factor rate 1.30, so list fee £6,000 per deal
Average net factor rate after discounts, rebates and waivers: 1.25, so net fee (the 'price') £5,000 per deal
Holdback 10% of daily card takings; typical repayment in about 8 months
Variable cost per deal £3,500: broker commission £1,600 (8% of advance), cost of funds £600, expected credit loss £1,000, servicing and collections £300
1,000 deals per year; fixed costs £1,000,000 per year
Annual baseline: gross list fees £6.0m, discounts and deductions £1.0m, net revenue £5.0m, variable cost £3.5m, contribution £1.5m, operating profit £0.5m
A 5% price increase means net fee £5,000 to £5,250 (net factor rate 1.25 to 1.2625)

w1-c1.title: Five different profit measures
w1-c1.oneLiner: Name the measure you're optimising - revenue, gross profit, contribution, operating profit and cash can disagree.
w1-c1.explainer: Revenue is what customers pay. Gross profit subtracts cost of goods sold. Contribution subtracts every cost that moves with volume (including variable selling, servicing and payment costs), so it shows what one more sale adds towards fixed costs. Operating profit also subtracts fixed operating costs. Cash is about timing: a profitable sale on 90-day terms still drains cash today. A pricing recommendation should say which of these it maximises, because they can point in different directions.
w1-c1.quickExample: A price cut can raise revenue while lowering contribution, if the extra customers are expensive to serve or the lost margin per unit outweighs the extra units.
w1-c1.lendingLens: For a merchant cash advance (MCA), fee income is the revenue line, but the real economics come after partner/broker commission, cost of funds and expected credit loss. Cash timing depends on how fast the holdback repays the advance.

example.setup: Harbour Lane, per deal: net fee £5,000, cost of funds £600, expected loss £1,000, broker commission £1,600, servicing £300. Fixed costs £1.0m on 1,000 deals.
steps: Gross profit (lender-style: fee minus funding cost and credit loss) = 5,000 - 600 - 1,000 = £3,400 per deal
Contribution (minus all variable costs) = 5,000 - 3,500 = £1,500 per deal, £1.5m a year
Operating profit = 1.5m - 1.0m = £0.5m
Cash: the £20,000 advance leaves on day 1 and the fee arrives over about 8 months, so a fast-growing book can be profitable and cash-negative at the same time
example.result: Same deal, four different numbers: £5,000 revenue, £3,400 gross profit, £1,500 contribution, and a cash outflow in month one.

w1-c2.title: Margin vs markup
w1-c2.oneLiner: Same profit, different denominator: margin divides by price, markup by cost.
w1-c2.explainer: If price is 100 and cost is 60, profit is 40. Margin = 40/100 = 40%. Markup = 40/60 = 66.7%. Mixing them up is one of the most common pricing errors: someone told to 'add a 40% margin' who adds 40% to cost (price 84) actually earns a 28.6% margin. Convert with markup = margin / (1 - margin) and margin = markup / (1 + markup).
w1-c2.quickExample: Cost 60, target 40% margin: price = 60 / (1 - 0.40) = 100. Cost 60 plus a 40% markup: price = 84, margin 28.6%.

example.setup: Net fee £5,000, variable cost £3,500.
steps: Profit per deal = 5,000 - 3,500 = £1,500
example.result: 30% margin and 42.9% markup describe the same deal. Pricing at cost + 30% would give a fee of £4,550 and only a 23.1% margin.

w1-c3.title: Price changes work through unit economics AND volume
w1-c3.oneLiner: A price move changes profit per unit and the number of units - you need both to judge it.
w1-c3.explainer: Raising price increases contribution per unit but usually loses some customers. The key question is how much volume you can lose before total contribution falls. With contribution margin CM% and a price change dP (both as fractions of the old price), the break-even volume change is -dP / (CM% + dP). Because the price change lands entirely on contribution, low-margin businesses are very sensitive to price, and price cuts need far more extra volume than price increases can afford to lose.
w1-c3.quickExample: Contribution margin 40%. A 5% increase breaks even if you lose up to 11.1% of volume (0.05/0.45). A 5% cut needs 14.3% more volume (0.05/0.35) just to stand still.

example.setup: 5% price increase: net fee £5,000 to £5,250. Variable cost stays £3,500. Baseline 1,000 deals.
steps: Unit contribution £1,500 to £1,750: +16.7% from a 5% price rise
Volume that keeps total contribution at £1.5m = 1,000 x 1,500 / 1,750 = 857 deals
Break-even volume loss = 1 - 1,500 / 1,750 = 14.3%
example.result: The increase pays off unless Harbour Lane loses more than about 14% of deals.

w1-c4.title: Relevant costs
w1-c4.oneLiner: Only costs that change because of the decision belong in the decision.
w1-c4.explainer: For a pricing decision, include costs that move with it: materials, transaction costs, servicing, commissions, and any fixed costs that genuinely change (new staff, new systems). Sunk costs and overheads that stay the same whatever you decide are irrelevant to the short-run choice. But allocated cost still matters over the long run: if every product is priced only above variable cost, nothing pays for the building, the tech team or management, and the business shrinks.
w1-c4.quickExample: Accepting a one-off order with spare capacity: the relevant cost is the extra materials and labour, not a share of factory depreciation.
w1-c4.lendingLens: Per deal, cost of funds, expected loss and commission are relevant. Head-office overhead is not relevant to one deal's price, but the whole book must cover it.

example.setup: A broker asks for factor rate 1.22 on a £20,000 renewal. Variable cost £3,500. Fixed costs £1.0m over 1,000 deals = £1,000 allocated per deal.
steps: Contribution = 4,400 - 3,500 = +£900, so the deal adds profit this year
Fully allocated cost = 3,500 + 1,000 = £4,500, so it 'loses' £100 on a fully loaded view
example.result: Worth doing if capital is not constrained and it will not reset every broker's expectations. As a standard price it would not cover fixed costs.

w1-c5.title: The price and margin waterfall
w1-c5.oneLiner: Step from list price down through every deduction to what you actually keep: pocket price.
w1-c5.explainer: List price is rarely what you earn. On-invoice deductions (standard and negotiated discounts) take you to invoice price. Off-invoice items (rebates, free freight, extended payment terms, co-op marketing, special service) take you to pocket price. Subtract variable cost to get pocket margin. Off-invoice items are often booked in other cost centres, so nobody sees the total leakage until someone draws the waterfall per customer or deal.
w1-c5.quickExample: List 100 - discount 8 = invoice 92. Then rebate 3, payment terms 1.50, freight 2, co-op marketing 1.50 = pocket price 84. With cost 60, pocket margin is 24, not the 40 the list price suggests.

example.setup: One £20,000 advance at list factor rate 1.30.
steps: List fee: £6,000
Negotiated rate discount to 1.275: -£500, invoice fee £5,500
Early-repayment rebate: -£300
Renewal fee waiver: -£200, pocket price £5,000
Variable costs: -£3,500, pocket margin £1,500
example.result: The merchant was quoted £6,000 but Harbour Lane pockets £5,000 and keeps £1,500, which is 25% of the list fee.

w2-c1.title: The demand curve
w2-c1.oneLiner: Price vs quantity, with everything else held still - which real data never does.
w2-c1.explainer: A demand curve answers: if only the price changed, how many units would customers buy? 'Holding other factors constant' is the hard part. In real data, income, competitor prices, promotions, seasonality and stock availability all move at the same time as price. Moving along the curve (a price change) is different from the curve shifting (demand itself rising or falling). Confusing the two is the root of most bad elasticity estimates.
w2-c1.quickExample: Ice-cream sales rise in summer even if you raise prices. That is the curve shifting out, not customers liking higher prices.

example.setup: Harbour Lane funds 1,000 deals at a £5,000 fee.
steps: Along the curve: at a £6,000 fee, with everything else unchanged, demand might be 900 deals
Shift of the curve: a competitor launches 24-hour funding and demand at £5,000 drops to 920
example.result: If both happen in the same quarter, observed volume might fall to about 830, and you cannot read the price effect straight off the data.

w2-c2.title: Own-price elasticity
w2-c2.oneLiner: Elasticity = % change in quantity / % change in price. Usually negative.
w2-c2.explainer: An elasticity of -2 means a 1% price rise loses about 2% of volume. If the absolute value is above 1, demand is elastic: volume moves more than price, so raising price cuts revenue. Below 1, demand is inelastic: raising price raises revenue. But revenue is not profit. Even elastic demand can make a price rise profitable if margins are thin, because the units you lose were barely profitable. Compare the elasticity to the break-even elasticity from your margin.
w2-c2.quickExample: At elasticity -0.5, a 10% rise loses about 5% of volume and revenue rises about 4.5%. At -2.0, it loses about 20% and revenue falls about 12%.

example.setup: Fee £5,000 to £6,000, deals 1,000 to 900. Arc method uses midpoints.
example.result: Inelastic on fee: revenue rises from £5.0m to £5.4m. Measured on the factor rate, the same data would give about -2.7.

w2-c3.title: Cross-price and income elasticity
w2-c3.oneLiner: Cross-price shows which products compete or go together; income elasticity shows recession exposure.
w2-c3.explainer: Cross-price elasticity is the % change in demand for A when B's price changes 1%. Positive means substitutes (B gets dearer, people switch to A). Negative means complements (B gets dearer, people buy less of both). Within your own range this tells you about cannibalisation. Income elasticity is the % change in demand per 1% change in customer income. High positive values mean demand rises fast in booms and falls hard in downturns.
w2-c3.quickExample: If a competitor's price rises 10% and your volume rises 4%, cross-price elasticity is +0.4: you are substitutes.

example.setup: A competitor cuts its fee on £20,000 from £5,600 (1.28) to £4,800 (1.24). Harbour Lane deals fall from 1,000 to 950. Arc method.
steps: Cross elasticity = -5.1 / -15.4 = +0.33
example.result: Positive, so the products are substitutes, but only weakly. A large competitor cut moved a small share of volume.

w2-c4.title: Elasticity is not one number
w2-c4.oneLiner: Different customers, channels and horizons respond differently - a single average hides that.
w2-c4.explainer: Customers with good alternatives and low switching costs are more elastic. Online channels where comparison is easy tend to be more elastic than relationship-led channels. Elasticity usually rises (in absolute terms) at higher price levels and over longer horizons, because customers take time to notice, search and switch. A blended average can make a price rise look safe overall while it drives away a valuable, price-sensitive segment.
w2-c4.quickExample: Short-run elasticity after a petrol price rise is low; over years people buy smaller cars, so the long-run response is much bigger.

example.setup: Harbour Lane estimates elasticity of -1.5 for broker deals (700 a year) and -0.3 for direct renewals (300 a year). Consider a 5% price rise.
steps: Broker deals: -1.5 x 5% = -7.5%, about 52-53 deals lost
Renewals: -0.3 x 5% = -1.5%, about 4-5 deals lost
Blended loss: about 57 of 1,000 = -5.7%
example.result: The blended view says 'mildly elastic'. The segment view says the rise is very safe on renewals and riskier on broker deals.

w2-c5.title: Correlation is not price effect
w2-c5.oneLiner: Before blaming (or crediting) price, rule out promotions, stock-outs, competitors and season.
w2-c5.explainer: Firms often set prices in response to demand: raising them when demand is strong, discounting when it's weak. That makes price and volume move together for reasons other than cause and effect, biasing naive estimates towards zero or even making them positive. This is called endogeneity. You need controls for the other drivers, a comparison group, or a controlled test (Week 8) before claiming a causal elasticity.
w2-c5.quickExample: A retailer raised prices in December and sales went up. That's Christmas demand, not a positive elasticity.
w2-c5.lendingLens: In lending, price also changes who accepts. If riskier merchants are more willing to accept a higher factor rate, a price rise can keep take-up steady while worsening the loss rate of the book. Watch mix and losses, not just volume.

example.setup: Harbour Lane raised rates in March and deals fell 15% month on month. In the same March, a major broker paused submissions, and last year March volume fell 10% with no price change.
steps: Seasonal pattern alone explains about -10%
The broker pause explains part of the rest
The remaining 'price effect' is at most about -5%, and possibly close to zero
example.result: Reading -15% as the price effect would overstate elasticity about threefold.

w3-c1.title: Economic value to the customer (EVC)
w3-c1.oneLiner: EVC = price of the next best alternative + what makes you better - what makes you worse.
w3-c1.explainer: Start with what the customer would pay for their best alternative (the reference value). Add positive differentiation value: measurable benefits you deliver that the alternative doesn't (time saved, revenue gained, risk avoided). Subtract negative differentiation value: things that are worse (switching cost, longer setup, missing features). The result is the most a rational, informed customer should pay. Pricing at EVC leaves them indifferent, so you normally price somewhere between the alternative and EVC, sharing the value.
w3-c1.quickExample: Competitor costs 10k a year. Your product saves 4k of staff time but needs 1k of extra training. EVC = 10 + 4 - 1 = 13k. A price around 11-12k gives the customer a clear reason to switch.
w3-c1.lendingLens: For an SME the alternatives might be an overdraft, a term loan, a card, another revenue-based funder, or not borrowing. Positive differentiation: speed, repayments that flex with sales, no fixed term. Negative: higher total cost.

example.setup: Next best alternative for a £20,000 need: an online term loan with total cost £4,000. Holdback flexibility (repayments fall in slow weeks, avoiding overdraft fees) is worth £900. Funding in 24 hours instead of 7 days lets the merchant take a £800 supplier discount. Daily remittance admin costs them £200.
steps: Reference value: £4,000
Positive differentiation: +£900 + £800 = +£1,700
Negative differentiation: -£200
example.result: The £5,000 net fee leaves the merchant £500 of value for switching. The £6,000 list fee is above EVC.

w3-c2.title: Willingness to pay is a distribution
w3-c2.oneLiner: Every customer has a different maximum price - think in curves, not single numbers.
w3-c2.explainer: Different customers value the same product differently. Lined up from highest to lowest willingness to pay, they form your demand curve. Any single price loses customers below it and leaves money on the table with customers above it. That gap is why segmentation, tiers and fences (Week 4) exist. Research should estimate the shape of the distribution, not just an average.
w3-c2.quickExample: If WTP ranges from 50 to 200, pricing at 100 loses everyone below 100 and undercharges everyone who would have paid up to 200.

example.setup: From past offers on £20,000: 80% of merchants accept at 1.22 (fee £4,400), 50% at 1.28 (£5,600), 20% at 1.35 (£7,000). Variable cost £3,500. Per 100 quotes:
example.result: The middle price wins on contribution. The 'average WTP' alone would not tell you that.

w3-c3.title: WTP research methods
w3-c3.oneLiner: Pick the method by the decision: price point, acceptable range, or feature trade-off.
w3-c3.explainer: Gabor-Granger asks whether you would buy at a series of prices, giving a simple demand curve for a known product. Van Westendorp asks four questions (too cheap, a bargain, getting expensive, too expensive) to find an acceptable range; it says nothing about how many will buy. Conjoint analysis has respondents trade off product profiles so you can estimate the value of each feature, including price. Discrete choice (choice-based conjoint) asks them to pick between realistic options, including 'none', which is closest to a real purchase.
w3-c3.quickExample: Setting the price of an existing product: Gabor-Granger. Deciding what goes in a premium tier: conjoint. Sanity-checking a range for a new concept: Van Westendorp.

example.setup: Decision: should the standard MCA offer have a 10% or a 15% holdback, and how much should the factor rate differ between them?
steps: Gabor-Granger: no, it tests price for one fixed package
Van Westendorp: no, it gives a price range without the trade-off
Choice-based conjoint: yes. Suppose it shows merchants treat a 15% holdback as worth about 0.03 of factor rate (£600 on £20,000)
example.result: A Fast offer at 15% holdback would need to be priced about 0.03 below Standard to be equally attractive.

w3-c4.title: Stated vs revealed preference
w3-c4.oneLiner: People say they'd pay more than they do - and buyers sometimes lowball on purpose.
w3-c4.explainer: Hypothetical bias: with no money on the line, respondents overstate what they'd pay. Strategic response: savvy buyers (especially B2B procurement) understate WTP to push your price down. Reduce both with realistic choice tasks instead of direct 'what would you pay' questions, including a 'none' option, reminding respondents of their budget, and validating survey results against real purchase data or a small live test.
w3-c4.quickExample: A survey says 60% would pay 20. At launch, 15% take it. That gap is typical of hypothetical bias.

example.setup: A merchant survey says 60% would accept a 1.30 factor rate. In the past, real offers at 1.30 were accepted 35% of the time.
steps: Calibration ratio = 35 / 60 = 0.58
Apply it to a new stated result: 50% stated at 1.32 gives about 29% expected actual acceptance
example.result: Using raw stated intent would overstate volume by about 70%.

w3-c5.title: Value communication
w3-c5.oneLiner: Customers pay for value they can see, not value that exists.
w3-c5.explainer: EVC is what an informed customer would pay. Real customers often don't know how much time you save or risk you remove, so their perceived value sits below economic value. Quantified case studies, ROI calculators, trials and guarantees close that gap. This matters most for new categories or benefits that are indirect, delayed or hard to measure.
w3-c5.quickExample: A tool that cuts invoice errors by 30% is worth more if sales can show the customer what errors currently cost them.

example.setup: A merchant compares a 1.25 factor rate with an online loan 'at 18% APR' and assumes the MCA is the costlier option.
steps: Show total cost in pounds: MCA £5,000 vs loan £4,000
Show the cash-flow difference: in a slow month with card takings down 40%, the holdback falls 40%; the loan payment does not
Quantify it with their data: avoided overdraft fees of about £900
example.result: An honest comparison in pounds and cash flow supports the £1,000 premium better than a headline rate that looks bad on its own.

w4-c1.title: Useful pricing segments
w4-c1.oneLiner: A segment is only useful for pricing if it differs AND you can tell who's in it at the point of sale.
w4-c1.explainer: Marketing segments based on attitudes ('innovators', 'price-conscious') are hard to use in pricing because you can't see them on a quote. Pricing segments must be observable when the deal happens: company size, industry, channel, order volume, contract length, usage, tenure. They must also differ in something that matters to price - willingness to pay, cost to serve, behaviour or value received. If either test fails, the segment can't support a different price.
w4-c1.quickExample: 'Values premium service' is not usable. 'Requests same-day delivery' is, because it's on the order.

example.setup: Candidate segment variables for Harbour Lane.
steps: New vs renewal: known at quote, differs in WTP and risk. Usable
Monthly card turnover (from processor data): known, linked to risk and cost to serve. Usable
How urgently the merchant needs cash: matters for WTP but is not observable. Not usable directly
Broker vs direct: known, differs in cost (commission) and price sensitivity. Usable
example.result: Three of the four can drive price. Urgency can only be captured indirectly, for example through a paid fast-funding option.

w4-c2.title: Price fences
w4-c2.oneLiner: Fences are the rules that stop high-WTP customers buying at the low price.
w4-c2.explainer: Fences come in a few types. Product fences: different versions (basic vs pro). Buyer fences: who you are (student, new customer, small business). Transaction fences: when or how you buy (advance purchase, volume, annual commitment, channel). Controlled availability: limited stock at a price. A good fence is easy to verify, hard to fake and feels fair. A weak fence (self-declared status with no check) leaks revenue through misrepresentation or resale.
w4-c2.quickExample: Airline advance-purchase fares fence out business travellers, who book late and won't commit early.

example.setup: Harbour Lane offers a renewal factor rate of 1.22 (vs 1.25 standard). Fence: at least 50% of the current advance repaid and no missed remittances in the last 90 days.
steps: Without a fence, assume 40% of 700 broker deals claim 'renewal-like' terms: 280 x £600 = £168,000 of fee given away
With the fence, only qualifying renewals (about 300 a year) get it, and they also carry lower risk
example.result: A precise fence keeps the renewal discount targeted at the merchants it is meant for.

w4-c3.title: Pricing models
w4-c3.oneLiner: Match the model to how customers get value: tiers, bundles, usage, subscription or fixed + usage.
w4-c3.explainer: Good-better-best tiers let customers self-select by WTP. Bundles sell items together; they work best when customers value the parts differently (negatively correlated WTP). Usage pricing charges per unit consumed and scales with value. Subscriptions charge for ongoing access. A two-part tariff combines a fixed fee with a usage price, capturing value from both light and heavy users. The value metric - what you charge per - should grow with the value the customer gets.
w4-c3.quickExample: Customer A values X at 8 and Y at 3; B values X at 5 and Y at 6. Best separate prices earn 16; a bundle at 11 earns 22.

example.setup: Two-part tariff: £300 origination fee plus factor rate 1.235, compared with flat 1.25.
example.result: Same price at the average deal, but underwriting cost is recovered on small deals and large deals become more competitive.

w4-c4.title: Architecture should guide, not confuse
w4-c4.oneLiner: A good line-up makes the right choice obvious; too many options paralyse buyers and sales.
w4-c4.explainer: Tiers should have a clear target customer each and a clear reason to upgrade. Anchoring and the compromise effect mean a premium tier makes the middle look reasonable, and many customers pick the middle. But beyond three or four options, choice overload slows decisions and sales reps start improvising. Avoid a deliberately crippled entry tier - customers feel tricked and it damages trust.
w4-c4.quickExample: Three tiers where 60% of customers pick the middle one usually means the architecture is doing its job.

example.setup: Three MCA offers on £20,000.
steps: Flex: factor 1.30, 8% holdback. Lowest daily burden, for seasonal or tight-cash merchants
Standard: factor 1.25, 10% holdback
Fast: factor 1.22, 15% holdback. Cheapest total cost and quickest repayment, for high-turnover merchants
Compare the alternative: 5 rates x 4 holdbacks = 20 combinations brokers cannot explain
example.result: Three clear trade-offs (total cost vs daily cash burden) are easier to sell and still let merchants self-select.

w4-c5.title: Fairness, transparency and law
w4-c5.oneLiner: Price differences must be explainable, fair and legal - not based on protected characteristics.
w4-c5.explainer: Customers accept price differences tied to something they control or understand (volume, timing, features). They resent differences that feel arbitrary or exploitative. Law restricts discrimination on protected characteristics, and some sectors have rules on fair value and transparency. Even legal personalisation can damage trust if discovered. Test every fence by asking: could we explain this to a customer and a regulator?
w4-c5.quickExample: A volume discount is easy to defend. Charging more because a customer's device suggests they're wealthy is not.
w4-c5.lendingLens: Risk-based pricing tiers should use data observable at application (trading history, card turnover, sector) and be explainable. Avoid proxies for protected characteristics.

example.setup: A model suggests charging 0.02 more in certain postcodes, where merchants accept higher rates.
steps: Ask why: is it risk (defaults are higher, a cost-based reason) or fewer alternatives (exploiting weaker bargaining power)?
Check whether postcode is acting as a proxy for a protected characteristic
If risk is the reason, price on the risk variables directly and document it
example.result: Same intended margin, but based on a reason you can explain and defend.

w5-c1.title: Market structure and pricing power
w5-c1.oneLiner: How many rivals and how different you are decide how much room you have on price.
w5-c1.explainer: Perfect competition: identical products, many sellers, no pricing power. Monopolistic competition: many sellers with differentiated products, so some power from differentiation. Oligopoly: a few big players who watch and react to each other, so every price move invites a response. Monopoly: one seller, maximum power, often regulated. The more differentiated you are and the fewer close rivals, the more your price depends on your value rather than theirs.
w5-c1.quickExample: UK grocery is an oligopoly: a price cut by one large chain is quickly matched, so permanent share gains from price are rare.

example.setup: Harbour Lane's market.
steps: Broker channel: each deal is shopped to about 4 lenders, so it is close to competitive and pricing power is low
Direct renewals: the merchant knows Harbour Lane, switching takes effort, so pricing power is higher
Implication: differentiate on speed and service in the broker channel, and protect margin on renewals
example.result: One company, two different competitive situations, needing two pricing approaches.

w5-c2.title: Comparing like with like
w5-c2.oneLiner: Normalise before you compare - headline prices hide different offers, terms and customers.
w5-c2.explainer: A competitor's list price can be cheaper while their total cost to the customer is higher, or their offer smaller. Normalise for package size, included features, service level, contract length, payment terms, discounts and fees, and channel. Also check whether they target the same customers. An unadjusted list-price comparison is one of the most common reasons companies cut prices they didn't need to cut.
w5-c2.quickExample: Competitor A is 10% cheaper but excludes onboarding and support and requires a 3-year contract. Normalised, they may be more expensive.
w5-c2.lendingLens: A competitor quoting a 1.20 factor vs your 1.28 isn't comparable until you check holdback %, fees, early-settlement discounts, advance size, speed and eligibility.

example.setup: Competitor quotes factor 1.22 with a £400 origination fee and 15% holdback. Harbour Lane quotes 1.25, no fee, 10% holdback. Advance £20,000.
steps: Competitor total cost = 20,000 x 0.22 + 400 = £4,800
Harbour Lane total cost = £5,000
Real gap = £200, not the £600 the factor rates suggest
The competitor's 15% holdback also takes 50% more cash per day from the merchant
example.result: On a like-for-like basis the competitor is only slightly cheaper and harder on the merchant's daily cash.

w5-c3.title: Game theory in pricing
w5-c3.oneLiner: Pricing is a repeated game: today's move shapes tomorrow's reaction.
w5-c3.explainer: In a one-off 'prisoner's dilemma', each firm is tempted to cut price, and both end up worse off. But competitors meet again and again, so reputations matter: firms that respond predictably to undercutting (tit-for-tat) discourage it. Credible commitments - like capacity or a publicly stated policy - change what rivals expect. Incumbents may price to deter entry. In some markets one firm acts as price leader and others follow. Use these ideas to predict reactions, not to coordinate with rivals.
w5-c3.quickExample: If you cut price 10% and your rival always matches within a week, you gain almost no share and both lose margin.

example.setup: Annual contribution for Harbour Lane and one rival, each choosing whether to hold 1.25 or cut to 1.20.
steps: Both hold: £1.5m each
One cuts: cutter £1.8m, holder £0.7m
Both cut: £0.9m each
In a one-shot game, cutting looks best whatever the rival does, so both end up at £0.9m
example.result: A credible, publicised policy of 'we match targeted cuts on renewals' makes cutting less attractive for the rival and can keep both at £1.5m.

w5-c4.title: Price wars
w5-c4.oneLiner: Diagnose why you lost share before cutting price - it's often not price at all.
w5-c4.explainer: Share loss can come from product gaps, stock-outs, service problems, a weak sales team, or losing a channel. Cutting price for any of those reasons sacrifices margin without fixing the cause, and invites retaliation. When responding to a competitor cut, compare: lost contribution from matching vs lost contribution from the volume you'd lose by not matching. Often a targeted response (specific segments or accounts) beats a broad one.
w5-c4.quickExample: Price 100, cost 60, 10,000 units. Competitor cuts 10%. Matching keeps volume but contribution falls to 300k. Not matching breaks even unless you lose more than 25% of volume.

example.setup: Harbour Lane lost 10% of broker deals in a quarter. Lost-deal analysis shows the winning lender funded in 24 hours vs Harbour Lane's 72, at a similar total cost.
steps: Price response: cut 5% across all 1,000 deals: 1,000 x £250 = £250,000 of contribution given up, and rivals may match
Service response: invest in 24-hour funding for broker deals
example.result: The problem was speed, so a price cut would have cost £250,000 without fixing it.

w5-c5.title: Competition law
w5-c5.oneLiner: Never discuss future pricing with competitors; be careful with signalling, parity clauses and resale price rules.
w5-c5.explainer: Agreeing prices with competitors (cartels) is illegal and can be criminal. Even sharing future pricing intentions, or exchanging competitively sensitive information through a third party, can breach the law. Public 'signalling' of intended price moves can raise concerns. Fixing the price at which resellers must sell (resale price maintenance) is usually prohibited. Price parity / most-favoured-nation clauses get regulatory scrutiny. Public competitor prices are fine to use. When unsure, involve legal - and know where those review points are.
w5-c5.quickExample: Chatting to a competitor at a conference about 'where rates are going next quarter' is a red line.

w6-c1.title: Pocket price beats list price
w6-c1.oneLiner: When discounts vary deal by deal, the list price tells you little - pocket price is what counts.
w6-c1.explainer: If every customer gets a different mix of discounts, rebates and terms, list price becomes a starting point for negotiation rather than the price. Plot pocket price for similar customers buying similar products and you usually see a wide spread - the pocket price band. That spread rarely lines up with deal size or customer value; it often reflects which rep handled the deal or how hard the customer pushed.
w6-c1.quickExample: Two customers of similar size buy the same volume. One pays a pocket price of 78, the other 91. The 13-point gap is negotiation, not value.

example.setup: Two £20,000 advances, both at list factor 1.30 (list fee £6,000).
steps: Merchant A: £300 rate discount, no rebate. Pocket £5,700
Merchant B: £800 rate discount, £400 early-repayment rebate, £200 renewal waiver. Pocket £4,600
Gap: £1,100 on identical list prices
example.result: A 2% list increase (£120) is small next to £1,100 of variance in what is actually realised.

w6-c2.title: Finding leakage with the waterfall
w6-c2.oneLiner: Slice the waterfall by rep, customer, product and channel to see exactly where price leaks.
w6-c2.explainer: The Week 1 waterfall becomes a diagnostic tool when you cut it by dimension. By rep: who discounts most for similar deals. By customer: who gets rebates they don't earn. By deduction type: which item (payment terms, freight, promotions) grows fastest. By channel: where partners take more than agreed. The goal is to separate earned deductions (tied to a customer commitment) from habitual leakage.
w6-c2.quickExample: Freight is waived on 70% of small orders, though policy says only above 500. That's a process leak worth fixing before any price change.
w6-c2.lendingLens: Lending leakage: commission overrides to brokers or partners, fees waived at renewal, unpriced early-settlement discounts, and advances rounded up beyond the approved amount.

example.setup: Comparable £20,000 deals, same risk grade. Broker A's average pocket fee is £5,400. Broker B's is £4,700 across 200 deals a year.
steps: Annual leakage if B matched A = 200 x 700 = £140,000
Check: is B's discount buying anything, such as lower risk or faster repayment? If not, it is leakage
example.result: One broker relationship holds £140,000 of contribution, almost a tenth of the company's total.

w6-c3.title: Making policy operational
w6-c3.oneLiner: Corridors, floors, approval levels and exception codes turn a pricing policy into rules reps can follow.
w6-c3.explainer: A discount corridor sets the normal range for a type of deal (by segment, size, term). Green: rep can approve. Amber: manager approval. Red: deal desk or finance. A floor price is the level below which no deal goes. Exception codes record why an out-of-policy deal was approved ('competitive', 'strategic logo', 'volume commitment'), so you can learn from patterns. Without these, policy lives in a slide deck and nowhere else.
w6-c3.quickExample: Corridor: 0-10% green, 10-15% amber, above 15% deal desk. An 18% request goes to the deal desk with a reason code.

example.setup: Corridor for standard £20,000 broker deals (variable cost £3,500).
steps: Green, factor 1.27 or more: account manager approves
Amber, 1.24 to below 1.27: team lead approves, exception code required
Approval required, below 1.24: deal desk
Floor 1.20: fee £4,000, contribution £500. Below this only the CFO can approve
example.result: A salesperson knows instantly what they can offer and what they must justify.

w6-c4.title: Sales incentives
w6-c4.oneLiner: Pay reps on revenue and they'll discount to close; pay on margin and they'll defend price.
w6-c4.explainer: If commission is a % of revenue, a 10% discount reduces the rep's pay by only 10% of commission but may cut the company's contribution by 25% or more. Reps rationally trade margin for speed and certainty. Fixes include paying on gross margin or contribution, adding a price-realisation multiplier, or reducing commission on discounted deals. Changing incentives is usually more effective than tightening approvals alone.
w6-c4.quickExample: At a 40% margin, a 10% discount needs 33% more volume to break even - but costs the rep only 10% of their commission on that deal.

example.setup: An account manager is paid 1% of funded amount. Two £20,000 deals: one at 1.20, one at 1.30.
steps: Pay on each deal: 1% x 20,000 = £200, the same
Contribution (variable cost £3,500): £500 vs £2,500
example.result: The company earns five times more on one deal, but the salesperson is paid the same on both. An extra bonus based on fee above 1.25 would fix that.

w6-c5.title: Give-get negotiation
w6-c5.oneLiner: Never give a concession without getting something back.
w6-c5.explainer: Every discount should buy something of value: higher volume, longer term, upfront payment, faster decision, a case study, auto-renewal, reduced scope or service. Prepare the 'get' list before the negotiation. Trade small concessions for big commitments, concede slowly, and use non-price variables (payment terms, service level, implementation timing) before touching price. This protects margin and teaches customers that pushing on price alone doesn't work.
w6-c5.quickExample: 'We can do 5% if you commit to 24 months and pay annually upfront.'

example.setup: A merchant asks for 1.22 instead of 1.25 on £20,000, a £600 concession.
steps: Ask for a holdback of 13% instead of 10%: repayment about 2 months faster, freeing capital and cutting cost of funds by about £150
Or ask for direct renewal next time (no broker commission, about £1,600 saved on the renewal)
Or offer half: 1.235 (£300) with no conditions
example.result: A trade that recovers most of the £600 beats a flat discount.

w7-c1.title: When revenue management works
w7-c1.oneLiner: Fixed, perishable capacity + variable demand + customers booking at different times = revenue management territory.
w7-c1.explainer: Airlines and hotels are the classic cases: an empty seat or room tonight is worth nothing tomorrow, adding capacity is slow and expensive, demand swings, and price-sensitive leisure customers book early while less sensitive business customers book late. Revenue management sells the same capacity at different prices through booking classes, and decides how much capacity to protect for later, higher-paying demand. Without those conditions, simpler pricing usually works better.
w7-c1.quickExample: A hotel holds back rooms from the discount channel on weekdays near a conference, expecting late corporate bookings at higher rates.
w7-c1.lendingLens: Funding capacity works a bit like perishable inventory. When capital is constrained, each advance has an opportunity cost: allocate it to deals with the best risk-adjusted return per pound, not the most volume.

example.setup: Harbour Lane can fund £2m this month (100 deals of £20,000). At 1.25, 120 merchants want funding. Variable cost £3,500.
steps: At 1.25: 100 funded (capacity binds), contribution 100 x 1,500 = £150,000
At 1.28 (fee £5,600): demand falls to about 100, all funded, contribution 100 x 2,100 = £210,000
example.result: When capacity binds, a higher price loses no funded volume and adds £60,000.

w7-c2.title: Dynamic vs personalised pricing
w7-c2.oneLiner: Dynamic = price moves with market conditions. Personalised = price moves with who you are. Different risks.
w7-c2.explainer: Dynamic pricing reacts to demand, time, inventory or competitors; everyone sees the same price at the same moment. Customers broadly accept it when the logic is visible (peak vs off-peak). Personalised pricing uses data about the individual (history, location, device) so two people see different prices at the same time. It carries bigger fairness, transparency and legal risk, and can destroy trust if discovered, even when it's legal.
w7-c2.quickExample: Surge pricing during a storm is dynamic. Showing a higher price to someone whose browsing suggests urgency is personalised.

example.setup: Two ideas for Harbour Lane.
steps: Dynamic: when the monthly funding line is 90% used, standard rates rise from 1.25 to 1.27 for every new quote
Personalised: a merchant whose bank data shows a maxed overdraft is quoted 1.32 because they seem desperate
example.result: The first is defensible if explained. The second prices on vulnerability rather than risk or cost, and carries serious conduct and reputational risk.

w7-c3.title: Markdown optimisation
w7-c3.oneLiner: Mark down too early and you give away margin; too late and you're left with unsold stock.
w7-c3.explainer: For seasonal or perishable stock, the question is when and how deep to discount. Holding price protects margin on what sells but risks leftover stock that's worth little. Discounting earlier sells more but at lower margin. Compare expected total contribution, including salvage value of leftovers, across markdown paths. Sell-through (% of stock sold) is the key leading indicator.
w7-c3.quickExample: 100 units left, two weeks to go. Holding at 50 sells 60 (3,000; 40 units scrapped). Marking down to 35 sells 95 (3,325). The markdown wins if leftovers are worth less than the difference.

example.setup: A retailer has 200 winter jackets, 4 weeks left. At £80, 100 sell. At £60, 180 sell. Leftovers are cleared at £10.
example.result: The markdown earns £2,000 more even though each sale earns £20 less.

w7-c4.title: Optimal on paper vs in practice
w7-c4.oneLiner: The model's optimum assumes its forecast is right - real-world error, rivals and operations can break it.
w7-c4.explainer: An optimiser is only as good as its demand forecast. Forecasts are wrong, competitors react, customers cancel or no-show, and operations can't always deliver what the model assumes. Test recommendations under low, expected and high demand. Prefer prices that are robust across scenarios over ones that are optimal only in the base case. Also check that revenue-maximising and profit-maximising answers agree; they differ when variable costs matter.
w7-c4.quickExample: Price 8 sells 1,500 (revenue 12,000). Price 12 sells 900 (revenue 10,800). With variable cost 5, contribution is 4,500 vs 6,300 - the 'lower revenue' price is better.

example.setup: Capacity case: 1.28 beats 1.25 by £60,000 (see the revenue management concept). Now suppose the higher rate drives away the best merchants, so expected loss rises from £1,000 to £1,400 per deal.
example.result: 1.28 still wins, but by £20,000 rather than £60,000. A slightly worse risk mix would remove the gain entirely.

w7-c5.title: Guardrails
w7-c5.oneLiner: Set limits the algorithm can't cross: floors, ceilings, max change per period, fairness rules.
w7-c5.explainer: Guardrails keep automated pricing within commercially acceptable bounds. Typical ones: minimum margin or floor price, maximum price, maximum % change per day or week, no price rises during emergencies, consistent prices across channels where customers would notice, and rules against using sensitive data. They trade a little theoretical revenue for trust, brand protection and fewer embarrassing headlines.
w7-c5.quickExample: A rule capping daily price changes at 10% and freezing prices during a declared emergency.

example.setup: Guardrails for Harbour Lane's capacity-based pricing.
steps: Standard rate moves no more than 0.02 per month
Minimum contribution of £500 per deal (factor floor 1.20 on £20,000)
A renewal is never priced above the merchant's previous deal unless their risk grade has worsened
Any change of 0.03 or more goes to the pricing committee
example.result: The model can still respond to demand, but no merchant sees a sudden or unexplained jump.

w8-c1.title: A useful pricing dataset
w8-c1.oneLiner: Realised price, units, product, customer, time, channel, promos, availability, cost, market - or you can't separate price from everything else.
w8-c1.explainer: Elasticity estimates need the realised price customers actually paid, not list price. They also need the other things that move demand, so you can control for them: promotions, stock-outs, seasonality, competitor prices, channel. Cost is needed to translate volume effects into profit. Missing any of these usually means the estimate silently absorbs the effect of the missing variable.
w8-c1.quickExample: If stock-out days aren't recorded, a period with high prices and empty shelves looks like extreme price sensitivity.

example.setup: Minimum fields for an MCA pricing dataset.
steps: Quote: date, advance, factor rate, holdback %, broker, risk grade, new or renewal
Outcome: accepted?, funded?, days to repay, early repayment, default flag, renewal taken
Economics: commission paid, cost of funds, realised loss
Context: competitor rate if known, funding-line utilisation, sector, month
example.result: With declined quotes included, you can model acceptance against price. Without them you only see the deals you won.

w8-c2.title: Limits of regression
w8-c2.oneLiner: Regression only controls what you measured - omitted variables and reverse causality still bias it.
w8-c2.explainer: Omitted variable bias: something you didn't measure (a competitor's promotion, a marketing campaign) affects both price and volume. Reverse causality: you set price because of demand, so demand partly causes price, not just the other way round. Both bias the price coefficient, usually towards zero. Adding more controls helps only for the variables you can observe. For a causal answer you need variation in price that isn't driven by demand - ideally a test.
w8-c2.quickExample: Regions with strong demand got price rises first. Regression shows small elasticity, but that's because demand caused the price, not because customers don't care.

example.setup: Raw data shows merchants offered higher factor rates accept more often, which would imply positive elasticity.
steps: Why: riskier merchants are priced higher and also have fewer alternatives, so they accept more
Risk grade drives both price and acceptance
Adding risk grade to the regression: within each grade, higher rates reduce acceptance as expected
example.result: Without the risk control, the model would suggest raising prices increases volume, which is false.

w8-c3.title: Randomised price tests
w8-c3.oneLiner: Randomise who gets which price, and differences in outcome are caused by price.
w8-c3.explainer: Random assignment makes test and control groups alike on average in everything except price, so the difference in outcomes is the price effect. Decide the unit of assignment (customer, store, region, time period). Watch for contamination: customers seeing both prices, sales reps working both groups. Price tests also raise fairness concerns - customers comparing notes may object - so many firms test on new customers, new products, or across regions rather than individuals.
w8-c3.quickExample: Randomly assign new applicants to one of two price points for four weeks and compare conversion and contribution per applicant.
w8-c3.lendingLens: Lending tests have slow outcomes: losses and repayment speed take months to appear. Use leading indicators (take-up, early repayment velocity, early arrears) with pre-agreed guardrails, and check fairness and any regulatory rules first.

example.setup: Within each risk grade, broker quotes are randomly assigned 1.25 or 1.27 for six weeks.
steps: Assignment is random within grade, so risk mix is balanced
Compare acceptance, funded volume and contribution per quote between the two groups
Range is narrow (0.02), time-limited, and every quote is honoured
example.result: The difference in contribution per quote is a credible estimate of the price effect.

w8-c4.title: Quasi-experiments
w8-c4.oneLiner: When you can't randomise, build a credible comparison group instead.
w8-c4.explainer: Matched markets: change price in some markets and compare to similar unchanged markets. Difference-in-differences: compare the change over time in the treated group with the change in the control group; this removes shared trends but assumes the groups would have moved in parallel without the change. Synthetic control: build a weighted blend of untreated units that tracks the treated unit before the change. Phased (staggered) rollout: introduce the change in waves so later waves act as controls for earlier ones.
w8-c4.quickExample: Treatment region conversion 20% to 18%; control 21% to 20%. DiD effect = -2 - (-1) = -1 percentage point.

example.setup: Broker channel moves to 1.27. Direct channel stays at 1.25. Acceptance rates before and after:
steps: Treated (broker): 40% to 36%, change -4 pp
Control (direct): 42% to 41%, change -1 pp
Difference-in-differences = -4 - (-1) = -3 pp
example.result: The price rise is estimated to cut acceptance by 3 points, assuming both channels would otherwise have moved in parallel.

w8-c5.title: The measurement plan
w8-c5.oneLiner: Write down what result means launch, revise or reject - before you look at the data.
w8-c5.explainer: A good plan states the decision it supports, the primary metric (ideally incremental contribution, not conversion alone), the minimum detectable effect (the smallest effect worth detecting, which drives sample size), guardrail metrics that would stop the test (complaints, churn, loss rates), the duration, and the decision rule. Pre-committing stops people moving the goalposts after seeing the numbers.
w8-c5.quickExample: Rule of thumb for 80% power at 5% significance: n per group is about 16 x p(1-p) / d^2. Baseline 20% conversion, detect 2 points: about 6,400 per group.

example.setup: Test: +5% fee (unit contribution £1,500 to £1,750). Control acceptance 40%, treatment 37%.
steps: Contribution per quote, control = 0.40 x 1,500 = £600
Contribution per quote, treatment = 0.37 x 1,750 = £647.50
Difference: +£47.50 per quote
Decision rule set in advance: launch if at least +£30 per quote and 60-day missed-remittance rate up by no more than 0.5 pp
example.result: Acceptance fell, but contribution per quote rose, so the pre-agreed rule says launch if the risk guardrail holds.

w9-c1.title: Launch essentials
w9-c1.oneLiner: Effective date, who's affected, transition rules, systems, owners, escalation - or it isn't a plan.
w9-c1.explainer: Decide exactly when the new price applies and to whom: new customers, renewals, existing contracts. Set transition rules: grandfathering (existing customers keep old prices for a period), notice periods, and how in-flight quotes are honoured. List every system that must change (quoting, billing, CRM, websites, partner portals) and test before go-live. Every task needs a named owner, and there must be a clear route for problems on day one.
w9-c1.quickExample: New prices for new applications from 1 March; existing customers move at their next renewal; quotes issued before 1 March honoured for 30 days.
w9-c1.lendingLens: Think in cohorts: new merchants, renewing merchants, and partners who present offers. Each may need different timing, messaging and system changes.

example.setup: Harbour Lane's rate change.
steps: Effective date: 1 March for new broker quotes. Renewals from 1 April
Quotes issued before 1 March honoured for 14 days
Existing advances unchanged
Owners: pricing engine update (CTO, by 15 Feb), broker pack (Head of Partnerships, by 20 Feb), QA of first 50 deals (Pricing lead)
example.result: Everyone knows what changes, for whom, from when, and who to call if it goes wrong.

w9-c2.title: Customer communication
w9-c2.oneLiner: Explain the change honestly, link it to value, and don't let anyone promise what you can't prove.
w9-c2.explainer: Tell customers what changes, when, and why, in plain language. Link it to value delivered, not just your costs. Give enough notice to be fair (and meet any contractual terms). Customer-facing teams need approved messaging so they don't improvise claims ('this is the lowest price in the market') that can't be supported and may create legal or trust problems.
w9-c2.quickExample: Better: 'From 1 March, the fee rises 4% to fund faster payouts, now same day.' Worse: 'Costs went up so prices go up.'

example.setup: Broker notice for a move from 1.25 to 1.27.
steps: Clear: 'From 1 March, standard factor rates for new advances move from 1.25 to 1.27. On £20,000, total cost changes from £5,000 to £5,400.'
Value: 'Funding within 24 hours and holdbacks that fall automatically in slow weeks are unchanged.'
Avoid: 'Still the cheapest MCA in the UK' (unless proven)
example.result: Brokers can repeat the message accurately, and nothing in it is a claim you cannot support.

w9-c3.title: Sales enablement
w9-c3.oneLiner: Reps need words, answers to objections, the rules, examples and practice - not just an email.
w9-c3.explainer: A talk track gives reps a short, consistent way to explain the change. Objection handling prepares answers for the predictable pushback ('too expensive', 'competitor is cheaper', 'we've been loyal'). Reps need the updated approval rules and corridors, worked deal examples, and role-play practice before they face customers. Under-prepared reps fall back on discounting, which erases the price change.
w9-c3.quickExample: Objection 'too expensive': acknowledge, ask what they're comparing against, reframe on outcomes, and only trade price for a commitment.

example.setup: Likely objection: 'Another lender offered 1.24.'
steps: Normalise: 'Does that include an origination fee? What's their holdback?' (1.24 plus a £400 fee = £5,200 total, vs our 1.27 = £5,400)
Value: 24-hour funding and a holdback that falls in slow weeks
Give-get: 'I can do 1.255 if you move to a 13% holdback'
example.result: The salesperson compares fairly, explains the value, and trades rather than simply discounting.

w9-c4.title: Governance and decision rights
w9-c4.oneLiner: Be clear who decides list prices, discounts, promotions, exceptions and corrections.
w9-c4.explainer: Without clear decision rights, pricing drifts: sales grants exceptions, marketing runs promotions, finance pushes back, and nobody owns the outcome. A RACI matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) makes it explicit, with exactly one Accountable per decision. Exceptions should be logged with reasons and reviewed regularly; if the same exception keeps being approved, the policy is wrong and should change.
w9-c4.quickExample: 40% of deals use the 'competitive' exception. That's not an exception any more - it's the real price, and the corridor needs revisiting.

example.setup: Decision rights at Harbour Lane.
steps: List rates: pricing committee, reviewed quarterly
Discounts in green and amber: sales, with exception codes
Below 1.24: deal desk. Below 1.20: CFO
Trigger: if more than 20% of deals in a month use the same exception code, the policy is reviewed
example.result: Routine deals move fast, large concessions get scrutiny, and patterns in exceptions update the policy.

w9-c5.title: Performance tracking
w9-c5.oneLiner: Track each link in the chain separately, so you know whether the idea or the rollout failed.
w9-c5.explainer: If profit disappoints, you need to know why. Adoption: is the new price actually in the systems and on quotes? Realised price: did discounting erode it? Volume response: did customers react as predicted? Mix: did the customer or product mix shift? Retention: are existing customers leaving? Financial return: what's the net effect? If adoption or realisation failed, the hypothesis was never tested - that's implementation failure, not a bad idea.
w9-c5.quickExample: List price rose 5% in the system, but realised price rose only 1% because reps offset it with discounts. Fix enablement and incentives before concluding the price rise failed.

example.setup: Plan: +5% fee (£5,000 to £5,250). After 8 weeks contribution is below plan.
steps: Adoption: 92% of quotes at the new rate
Realised fee: £5,150, so only 60% of the planned +£250 stuck (extra amber discounts)
Volume: -4%, inside the -3% to -7% planning range
example.result: Customers behaved as expected. The shortfall comes from discounting, so this is an execution problem, not a pricing hypothesis problem.

w10-c1.title: What makes a recommendation decision-ready
w10-c1.oneLiner: Decision, money, customer logic, evidence, plan, risks - in that order, decision first.
w10-c1.explainer: Executives read the first page and decide whether to keep going. Lead with the decision you're asking for: the price change, scope, effective date and approval needed. Then the financial effect, why customers will accept it, the evidence behind your numbers, how it will be executed, and what could go wrong. This 'answer first' structure (often called the pyramid principle) respects the reader's time and makes the ask unmissable.
w10-c1.quickExample: Slide 1: 'Approve a 4% factor-rate increase for new merchants in tiers B-C from 1 March. Expected +X contribution in year 1; downside break-even if take-up falls more than Y%.'

example.setup: First line of the Harbour Lane recommendation.
steps: Decision: 'Approve a 5% increase in the standard net fee (factor rate 1.25 to 1.2625) for new broker and direct deals from 1 March.'
Effect: 'Base case +£137,500 incremental profit in year one, after £60,000 implementation cost.'
Risk: 'Loss-making if volume falls more than 10.9%. Planning range -3% to -7%.'
example.result: Decision, value and main risk in three sentences.

w10-c2.title: Scenarios and assumptions
w10-c2.oneLiner: Show base, downside and upside - and the assumptions that move between them.
w10-c2.explainer: A single number hides uncertainty. Show a base case plus downside and upside cases, each driven by stated assumptions (elasticity, competitor reaction, adoption, cost). A sensitivity analysis (often shown as a tornado chart) shows which assumption moves the answer most. Pair it with the break-even condition: how bad must the key assumption be before the decision is wrong? Decision-makers trust honest ranges more than false precision.
w10-c2.quickExample: 'We break even unless volume falls more than 11%. Our base case is -5%; the downside, assuming a competitor matches, is -9%.'

example.setup: +5% fee, unit contribution £1,750, baseline contribution £1.5m, implementation cost £60,000.
steps: Upside (0% volume): 1,000 x 1,750 = £1.75m. Incremental profit 250,000 - 60,000 = +£190,000
Downside (-12%): 880 x 1,750 = £1,540,000. Incremental profit -£20,000
Break-even: (1,500,000 + 60,000) / 1,750 = 891 deals, a volume loss of 10.9%
example.result: The case works unless volume falls by more than about 11%. That is the assumption to test first.

w10-c3.title: Learning after launch
w10-c3.oneLiner: Your estimate will be wrong - plan when you'll check and what would change your mind.
w10-c3.explainer: Build learning milestones into the plan: dates when you'll review leading indicators and pre-agreed triggers for each outcome. Stop if guardrails are breached (e.g. retention drops beyond a threshold). Adjust if a segment responds worse than expected. Expand if results beat the base case. This turns the recommendation from a one-off bet into a managed experiment and makes approval easier.
w10-c3.quickExample: Week 4 review: if take-up in tier C falls more than 10%, revert tier C; if under 3%, extend to tier D.

example.setup: Checkpoints for the Harbour Lane change.
steps: Week 4: realised fee at least £5,200, acceptance down no more than 5 pp, 30-day missed-remittance rate not up
Week 8: funded volume within -7% of baseline
Week 12: contribution per quote at or above plan. Decide to expand to renewals or hold
example.result: If week 4 shows realised fee at £5,100, you fix discount control before volume data is even in.

w10-c4.title: Facts, estimates, assumptions and choices
w10-c4.oneLiner: Label each claim: fact, estimate, assumption or choice - so people know what to challenge.
w10-c4.explainer: Facts are observed and verifiable (last year's volume). Estimates are derived from data with uncertainty (elasticity of -1.4). Assumptions are judgements without strong data (competitors won't react for 6 months). Management choices are value calls (protecting share in a strategic segment). Mixing them up makes a recommendation look more certain than it is and hides where debate should focus.
w10-c4.quickExample: 'Volume 10,000 (fact); elasticity -1.4 +/- 0.4 (estimate); no competitor response in Q1 (assumption); prioritise margin over share (choice).'

example.setup: Inputs to the Harbour Lane case.
steps: Fact: 1,000 deals funded last year at an average net fee of £5,000
Estimate: elasticity of about -0.6 (range -0.3 to -1.0)
Assumption: competitors will not follow within 6 months
Management choice: exempt renewals for the first quarter
example.result: Reviewers can see that the competitor-response assumption deserves the most challenge.

w1.summary: Price is usually the most powerful profit lever, but only if you know which profit measure you're optimising and how much volume you can afford to lose. This week gives you the arithmetic every later week depends on: margin vs markup, contribution, break-even volume change, relevant costs and the price waterfall.

workedExample.title: Week 1 exercise, worked
workedExample.setup: Price 100, variable cost 60, 10,000 units, fixed cost 250,000.
steps: Baseline: unit contribution 40, total contribution 400,000, operating profit 150,000.
+5% price: price 105, unit contribution 45.
Break-even volume = 10,000 x 40 / 45 = 8,889 units, a loss of 11.1%.
workedExample.takeaway: The increase pays unless you lose more than about 11% of volume. Fixed costs don't change the answer because they don't change with the decision.

w2.summary: Elasticity turns 'customers might leave' into a number you can put in a model. This week covers own-price, cross-price and income elasticity, how to estimate them, why estimates differ by segment and time horizon, and why a sales change after a price change is not automatically caused by the price.

workedExample.title: Arc elasticity and the break-even test
workedExample.setup: Price moves from 10 to 12; volume moves from 1,000 to 850. Contribution margin at the old price is 40%.
steps: % change in quantity (midpoint) = (850 - 1,000) / 925 = -16.2%.
% change in price (midpoint) = (12 - 10) / 11 = +18.2%.
Arc elasticity = -16.2 / 18.2 = -0.89.
Break-even volume loss for a 20% rise at 40% margin = 0.20 / 0.60 = 33.3%.
Actual loss was 15%, well inside 33.3%, so contribution rose.
workedExample.takeaway: Compare the volume you actually lose with the volume you can afford to lose. The elasticity only matters relative to your margin.

w3.summary: Cost sets the floor and value sets the ceiling. This week is about estimating the ceiling: economic value to the customer, how willingness to pay is distributed, which research method answers which question, and why what customers say often differs from what they do.

workedExample.title: EVC for one segment
workedExample.setup: Next best alternative costs 10,000 a year. Your product saves 160 staff hours a year at 25/hour and avoids 1,000 of errors. It needs 1,000 of extra training and has 1,000 of one-off switching cost, spread over 2 years.
steps: Reference value: 10,000.
Positive differentiation: 160 x 25 = 4,000 time saved, plus 1,000 errors avoided = 5,000.
Negative differentiation: training 1,000, plus switching 1,000 / 2 years = 500. Total 1,500.
Price range: above 10,000 (no reason to cut below the alternative) and well below 13,500 (customer needs an incentive to switch).
workedExample.takeaway: Label each line as observed, calculated or assumed. The error-avoidance figure is usually the weakest evidence.

w4.summary: Because willingness to pay varies, one price leaves money on the table. Price architecture - tiers, bundles, metrics and fences - lets different customers pay different amounts in a way that is fair, understandable and hard to game.

workedExample.title: Why bundling works
workedExample.setup: Two customers. A values X at 8 and Y at 3. B values X at 5 and Y at 6.
steps: Price X separately: at 5 both buy (10); at 8 only A buys (8). Best = 10.
Price Y separately: at 3 both buy (6); at 6 only B buys (6). Best = 6.
Total from separate pricing = 16.
Bundle: A values it at 11, B at 11. Price the bundle at 11 and both buy = 22.
Bundling adds 6 (+37.5%) because the two customers' preferences offset each other.
workedExample.takeaway: Bundling captures more value when WTPs are negatively correlated. If both customers valued both items similarly, bundling would add little.

w5.summary: Competitor prices are evidence, not instructions. This week covers market structure, comparing offers like-for-like, basic game theory, why price wars destroy value, how to diagnose whether a problem is really about price, and the legal lines around competitor information.

workedExample.title: Match or hold?
workedExample.setup: Your price 100, variable cost 60, 10,000 units. A competitor cuts their price 10%.
steps: Baseline contribution: 10,000 x 40 = 400,000.
Match (price 90): unit contribution 30. Even if volume holds, contribution = 300,000.
Hold (price 100): contribution = units retained x 40.
Holding is better unless units fall below 300,000 / 40 = 7,500 - a 25% loss.
Next step: estimate how many customers actually switch, by segment. If only one segment is at risk, a targeted response protects it without repricing everyone.
workedExample.takeaway: Matching is expensive. It's only right if you'd otherwise lose more volume than the break-even.

w6.summary: The price you set is not the price you get. This week is about the gap: waterfalls, pocket price bands, discount corridors, approval rules, sales incentives and negotiation. It's often the fastest source of margin improvement because no list price has to change.

workedExample.title: An illustrative MCA deal waterfall
workedExample.setup: Advance 50,000 at a 1.30 factor rate (illustrative numbers, not any lender's actual economics).
steps: Total repayable = 65,000. Gross fee = 15,000.
Partner/broker commission at 8% of advance: -4,000.
Expected credit loss at 5% of repayable: -3,250.
Cost of funds (average balance ~half the advance for ~9 months at 10%/yr): -1,875.
Underwriting and servicing: -500.
workedExample.takeaway: A third of the headline fee survives to contribution. Commission and loss assumptions move the answer far more than small factor-rate changes.

w7.summary: When capacity is fixed and perishable, the question changes from 'what price?' to 'which customers get the capacity, at what price, and when?'. This week covers revenue management, dynamic vs personalised pricing, markdowns, and the guardrails that stop an optimiser damaging trust.

workedExample.title: Littlewood's rule: how many seats to protect
workedExample.setup: Two fares: full 300, discount 100. Discount customers book first. How many seats should you hold back for full-fare customers?
steps: Selling one more seat at discount earns 100 for certain.
Holding that seat earns 300 only if full-fare demand exceeds the seats already protected.
Keep protecting seats while P(full-fare demand > protected seats) x 300 >= 100.
That means protect while the probability is at least 1/3.
If there's a 40% chance full-fare demand exceeds 20 seats, protect the 21st too; at 30%, sell it at discount.
workedExample.takeaway: The protection level depends on the fare ratio and the full-fare demand forecast - not on filling the plane.

w8.summary: Most pricing data is observational and confounded. This week covers what a usable pricing dataset contains, why regression alone can mislead, how to run tests or quasi-experiments when randomisation is hard, and how to write a measurement plan with a decision rule before you see the results.

workedExample.title: Why conversion isn't enough
workedExample.setup: Control: price 100, variable cost 60, 1,000 visitors, 20% convert. Test: price 110, 1,000 visitors, 17% convert.
steps: Conversion fell 3 points - looks like a loss.
Control contribution: 200 sales x 40 = 8,000.
Test contribution: 170 sales x 50 = 8,500.
Incremental contribution per visitor: +0.50 for the test.
Decision depends on whether that difference is bigger than the noise and whether guardrails (complaints, churn) held.
workedExample.takeaway: Judge price tests on contribution per eligible customer. Conversion and revenue can point the wrong way.

w9.summary: Good pricing decisions fail in execution all the time. This week covers launch logistics, customer communication, sales enablement, decision rights and exception governance, and a scorecard that tells you whether a disappointing result came from the idea or the rollout.

workedExample.title: Reading a launch scorecard
workedExample.setup: Planned (at a 40% contribution margin): +5% realised price, -4% volume, +8% contribution. Month 2 actuals below.
steps: Adoption: 98% of quotes on new price list. OK.
Realised price: +1.5% vs +5% plan. Problem.
Volume: -2% vs -4% plan. Better than expected.
Exception log: 'competitive' code on 35% of deals, up from 10%.
Diagnosis: implementation failure (discounting offset), not a flawed hypothesis - customers reacted less than feared.
workedExample.takeaway: Without separate adoption and realisation lines, this would have looked like 'the price rise didn't work'.

w10.summary: The capstone pulls everything together into a decision someone can actually make. This week covers how to structure a decision-ready recommendation, present scenarios and sensitivities honestly, build a profit bridge, separate facts from assumptions, and set triggers to stop, adjust or expand after launch.

workedExample.title: A profit bridge from price and volume
workedExample.setup: Baseline: price 100, variable cost 60, 10,000 units, contribution 400,000. New: price 105, volume 9,300.
steps: Price effect = price change x new volume = 5 x 9,300 = +46,500.
Volume effect = volume change x old unit contribution = -700 x 40 = -28,000.
Net = +18,500, matching the new contribution of 418,500.
If there were mix or cost changes, they'd be separate bars.
workedExample.takeaway: A bridge shows leadership exactly where the money comes from and reconciles back to the model - which is what the scoring guide checks.

w1.question: Net fee £5,000, variable cost £3,500. What is the margin %?
w1.explanation: Margin = (5,000 - 3,500) / 5,000 = 1,500 / 5,000 = 30.0%. Dividing by cost instead gives 42.9%, which is the markup.

w1.question: Same deal: net fee £5,000, variable cost £3,500. What is the markup %?
w1.explanation: Markup = (5,000 - 3,500) / 3,500 = 1,500 / 3,500 = 42.9%. Markup is always larger than margin because cost is smaller than price.

w1.question: Fee rises 5% from £5,000 to £5,250. Variable cost stays £3,500. What volume loss leaves total contribution unchanged?
w1.explanation: Unit contribution goes from £1,500 to £1,750. Break-even volume loss = 1 - 1,500 / 1,750 = 14.3%. Equivalent shortcut: price change / new unit contribution = 250 / 1,750.

w1.question: Baseline 1,000 deals. After a 5% fee rise, unit contribution is £1,750. What is total contribution if volume falls 7%?
w1.explanation: Volume = 1,000 x 0.93 = 930 deals. Contribution = 930 x 1,750 = £1,627,500, which is £127,500 above the £1.5m baseline.

w1.question: Which leakage item is best fixed by a process action rather than a pricing action?
options: The standard factor rate sits below customers' economic value
Operations applies early-repayment rebates automatically, even when the contract does not entitle the merchant
The renewal discount is larger than the risk difference justifies
A competitor has cut its headline rate
w1.explanation: The rebate is leaking because of how it is applied, not because of the price policy. Fix the system rule or approval step. The other three are pricing or strategy questions.

w1.question: You are deciding whether to accept one extra renewal at a discounted rate. Which cost is NOT relevant to that decision?
options: Cost of funds on the advance
w1.explanation: Rent does not change whether you do this deal or not, so it is not a relevant cost for this decision. The other three are incurred only if the advance is made.

w1.question: A 5% fee rise (£5,000 to £5,250) also attracts riskier merchants, so expected loss rises from £1,000 to £1,100 per deal. Other variable costs unchanged. What is the break-even volume loss now?
w1.explanation: Variable cost becomes £3,600, so new unit contribution = 5,250 - 3,600 = £1,650. Break-even loss = 1 - 1,500 / 1,650 = 9.1%. Adverse selection cuts the safety margin from 14.3% to 9.1%.

w1.question: Price 80, cost 60. What is the markup?
Contribution margin 40%. You raise price 5%. Which volume change makes total contribution fall?
w1.explanation: Break-even volume loss is 0.05 / 0.45 = 11.1%. Only the 12% loss exceeds it.

w1.question: You have spare capacity and are offered a one-off discounted order. Which cost is relevant?
w1.explanation: Only costs that change because you accept the order are relevant. The others are incurred either way.

w1.question: Unit contribution falls from 40 to 35. How many units keep contribution at the 10,000-unit level?
Two MCAs both have a 1.30 factor rate. A repays in 6 months, B in 12. Ignoring losses, which is true?
w1.explanation: The same fee earned over half the time means a much higher annualised return. The factor rate alone doesn't tell you the yield.
options: A has the higher annualised return
B has the higher annualised return
You can't compare them without the advance size

w1.question: Rebates are being paid to customers who never hit the volume target. What kind of fix does this need?
w1.explanation: The policy is fine; execution is leaking. That's a process fix.
options: A pricing action: lower list prices
A process action: enforce rebate eligibility
A cost action: cut variable cost

w1.question: Price 100, variable cost 60, 10,000 units. Price +5%, volume -7%. New total contribution, in thousands?
List 100. On-invoice discount 8, rebate 3, payment terms cost 1.50, freight 2, co-op marketing 1.50. Pocket price?
Target margin 35% on a cost of 65. What price?

w2.question: Fee rises from £5,000 to £6,000 and deals fall from 1,000 to 900. What is the arc (midpoint) elasticity?
Product A has elasticity -0.5 and product B has -2.0. You raise both prices by 4%. What happens to revenue?
w2.explanation: A: volume -2%, price +4%, so revenue rises about 2%. B: volume -8%, price +4%, so revenue falls about 4%. Note that contribution can still rise for B if margins are thin. Revenue is not profit.

w2.question: The cross-price elasticity between your MCA and a competitor's loan is +0.33. What does this tell you?
w2.explanation: Positive cross elasticity means that when their price falls, your volume falls: substitutes. 0.33 is small, so a 10% competitor cut costs you only about 3% of volume. It says nothing about your own-price elasticity.

w2.question: Elasticity is -1.5. You raise the fee by 4%. What volume change do you expect (simple approximation)?
w2.explanation: %ΔQ ≈ elasticity x %ΔP = -1.5 x 4% = -6.0%. This approximation holds for small changes within the observed price range.

w2.question: Deals fell 15% the month after a rate rise. The same month a large broker paused submissions, and that month always dips about 10%. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: Elasticity is high: the price rise cut volume 15%
The price effect is at most about 5%, and could be smaller
The price rise had no effect at all
The broker pause caused the whole fall
w2.explanation: Seasonality explains about 10 points, and the broker pause explains some of the rest. The price effect is whatever is left, at most about 5%. You cannot claim zero or the full 15% without a comparison group.

w2.question: Deals fall 10% when the factor rate goes from 1.25 to 1.30. Which statement is correct (simple % changes)?
options: Elasticity is -2.5 whichever way you measure price
Elasticity is about -2.5 on the factor rate and -0.5 on the fee; you must state which you use
Elasticity is -0.5 on the factor rate and -2.5 on the fee
Elasticity cannot be calculated for an MCA
w2.explanation: Factor rate: +4% (0.05 / 1.25), so -10 / 4 = -2.5. Fee: £5,000 to £6,000 is +20%, so -10 / 20 = -0.5. Same data, five times the number. Define price before quoting an elasticity.

w2.question: Why might elasticity measured between 1.22 and 1.28 be misleading for a move to 1.35?
options: Elasticity is always constant along a demand curve
Above some price, cheaper alternatives such as term loans become attractive, so the response can get much stronger
w2.explanation: Demand responds to thresholds. Once your price passes a competitor's or an alternative's total cost, many customers switch at once. Data from one range does not tell you about behaviour outside it.

w2.question: Elasticity is -0.5. You raise price 10%. What happens to revenue?
w2.explanation: Volume falls about 5%. Revenue = 1.10 x 0.95 = 1.045, up about 4.5%.

w2.question: Cross-price elasticity between A and B is +0.6. A and B are:
w2.explanation: When B's price rises, demand for A rises, so customers treat them as alternatives.

w2.question: A retailer raised prices in December and sales rose. The best explanation is:
w2.explanation: Christmas demand moved the whole curve. You can't read elasticity from this without controlling for season.
options: Seasonal demand shifted the curve, confounding the price effect
Elasticity is positive for this product

w2.question: Elasticity is -3. By the Lerner rule, the profit-maximising margin is about:
You raise factor rates 5% and offer take-up barely changes. What should you check before calling it a success?
w2.explanation: In lending, price can change who accepts. Riskier merchants may be less price-sensitive, so losses can rise even when volume holds.
options: Nothing, take-up is the key metric
Whether the risk mix and loss rates of accepted merchants changed

w2.question: Prices are typically raised when demand is strong. A naive regression of volume on price will most likely:
w2.explanation: High prices coincide with high demand, so the estimated slope is pulled towards zero or even positive.
options: Understate how elastic demand is (bias towards zero)

w2.question: Price 20 to 22, quantity 500 to 460. Arc elasticity (to 2 decimals)?
Contribution margin 30%. Price +10%. What is the break-even elasticity?

w3.question: Next best alternative costs £4,000. Positive differentiation is worth £1,700 and negative differentiation £200. What is EVC?
w3.explanation: EVC = reference value + positive differentiation - negative differentiation = 4,000 + 1,700 - 200 = £5,500.

w3.question: You need to decide how factor rate should trade off against holdback % and funding speed in a new package. Which method fits best?
w3.explanation: Conjoint and discrete choice measure trade-offs among several attributes and price. Gabor-Granger and Van Westendorp test price for a single fixed offer.

w3.question: What does a Van Westendorp study give you?
options: A range of prices customers find acceptable
The value of each product feature
w3.explanation: The four questions (too cheap, bargain, expensive, too expensive) give an acceptable price range. They do not measure how many people would actually buy at each price.

w3.question: Historically, actual acceptance runs at 0.6 times stated intent. A survey says 60% would accept 1.30. What acceptance should you plan for?
w3.explanation: Planned acceptance = 60% x 0.6 = 36%. Stated intent overstates real behaviour (hypothetical bias), so calibrate against past results.

w3.question: Willingness to pay is a distribution. What is the most useful practical consequence?
options: Set price at the average WTP
Every price captures a different share of customers, so compare contribution across price points and consider tiers or segment prices
Survey more customers until WTP becomes one number
Price at the highest WTP observed
